extracted.intended_audience: practitioners (auditors/accountants) engaged to examine or review Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) under PCAOB attestation standards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for practitioners performing examination or review attest engagements on MD&A prepared pursuant to SEC rules (e.g., Item 303 of Regulation S‑K), including engagement acceptance, planning, performance, and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to examination and review engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: This section is applicable when a practitioner is engaged to (a) examine an MD&A presentation of a public or qualifying nonpublic entity prepared pursuant to SEC rules, or (b) review an MD&A presentation for an annual, interim, or combined period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonpublic entities must provide a written assertion that the presentation has been prepared using the SEC rules. Practitioners performing agreed-upon procedures should follow section 201 guidance. See paragraph .02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement objective — examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner's objective in an engagement to examine MD&A is to express an opinion on the MD&A presentation taken as a whole by reporting whether: (a) the presentation includes, in all material respects, the required elements of the SEC rules; (b) the historical financial amounts have been accurately derived from the financial statements; and (c) the underlying information, determinations, estimates, and assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examination seeks to obtain reasonable assurance by accumulating sufficient evidence and to restrict attestation risk to an appropriately low level. See paragraphs .05 and .28.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement objective — review
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective of a review of MD&A is to report whether any information came to the practitioner's attention causing belief that: the MD&A does not include required SEC elements; historical financial amounts have not been accurately derived; or the underlying information, determinations, estimates, and assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis for disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review consists principally of analytical procedures and inquiries and ordinarily does not include inspection, observation, confirmation, or obtaining corroborating evidential matter. A review provides limited assurance and may not detect all significant matters. See paragraph .08.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precondition for acceptance — audit prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may accept an engagement to examine or review MD&A only if the practitioner has audited, in accordance with GAAS, the financial statements for at least the latest period to which the MD&A relates and the other periods covered have been audited by the practitioner or a predecessor auditor (with specified exceptions for interim/nonpublic conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This base knowledge from auditing historical financial statements is necessary to evaluate results of procedures for MD&A. See paragraphs .06, .09, .11-.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement acceptance considerations — management competence
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether to accept an engagement, the practitioner should consider whether management (and those engaged by management) has appropriate knowledge of the SEC rules and regulations to prepare MD&A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether management can interpret criteria, derive historical amounts, assess relevancy, and make reasonable estimates and assumptions. See paragraph .15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management responsibilities for MD&A
rubrics_metrics.description: Management is responsible for preparation of MD&A pursuant to the SEC rules, including interpreting criteria, accurately deriving historical amounts, determining relevancy of information, and making estimates and assumptions that affect reported information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner should obtain written assertion from management about responsibility (see paragraph .16 and paragraph .32 footnote guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on use of practitioner's name
rubrics_metrics.description: An entity should not name the practitioner in a client-prepared document as having examined or reviewed MD&A unless the MD&A presentation and related practitioner's report and related financial statements and auditor's (or accountant's review) report are included or incorporated by reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the client names the practitioner improperly, the practitioner should request removal or revise the document; if client does not comply, the practitioner should advise nonconsent and consider other actions (including legal counsel). See paragraph .17.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding of SEC rules and management's methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner should obtain an understanding of the SEC rules for MD&A and inquire of management about the method of preparing MD&A, including sources of information, how information is gathered, how management evaluates material factors (including liquidity and capital resources), and changes from prior year procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to paragraph .04 for specific SEC sources (Item 303 Reg S‑K, FRR No. 36, Item 9 Form 20‑F, etc.). See paragraphs .18-.19.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and coordination of procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper planning contributes to effectiveness; performing some MD&A work in conjunction with the audit of historical financial statements or review of interim financial statements may improve efficiency and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner may consider results of tests of controls, analytical procedures, and substantive tests from the financial statement audit or review. See paragraph .20.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality — scope and qualitative considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Materiality in MD&A planning and performance encompasses both material omissions (e.g., omitted trends, events, uncertainties) and material misstatements; assessing materiality may rely more on qualitative than quantitative considerations, and prospective information is judged in light of expected range of reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider relevance and reliability, qualitative aspects, and the effect on a reasonable person's decision; an individual assertion is material if its inclusion or correction would influence a reasonable user's view. See paragraphs .21-.22.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of pro forma financial information
rubrics_metrics.description: When management includes pro forma financial information in MD&A, the practitioner should consider section 401 guidance and, in an examination, obtain understanding of the underlying transaction, discuss assumptions with management, and obtain sufficient evidence supporting adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an examination, procedures ordinarily include understanding the transaction, discussing assumptions, and obtaining evidence even if the info was derived from unaudited statements; the practitioner opines on MD&A as a whole, not on pro forma information alone. See paragraph .23.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and testing of external information
rubrics_metrics.description: External information included in MD&A (e.g., debt ratings, trade association statistics) should be subjected to the practitioner's procedures; practitioner may compare such information to published sources but is not expected to test trade association calculations underlying statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate procedures to external information based on engagement type (examination vs review). See paragraph .24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and testing of forward‑looking information
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward‑looking disclosures included in MD&A should be subjected to procedures to express an opinion that the underlying information, determinations, estimates, and assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the disclosures; practitioner may consider section 301 guidance and whether meaningful cautionary language is included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward‑looking info is tested only for the reasonableness of basis for the disclosures; safe harbor rules under the Securities Acts may apply and legal questions may affect protection. See paragraphs .25‑.26.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of voluntary additional SEC information
rubrics_metrics.description: If MD&A includes voluntary information that is required by other SEC rules (e.g., Item 305 Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk), the practitioner should consider those other rules when subjecting that information to procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary information that draws in other SEC rules requires practitioner attention to those rules. See paragraph .27.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attestation risk components and assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: For examination engagements, practitioner plans procedures to obtain reasonable assurance of detecting material misstatements; components of attestation risk are inherent risk, control risk, and detection risk, and the practitioner assesses each to determine nature, timing, and extent of tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition that absolute assurance is unattainable; professional judgment required in assessing significant determinations and the sufficiency of persuasive (not always convincing) evidence. See paragraphs .29‑.33.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of assertions in MD&A
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions embodied in MD&A can be explicit or implicit and are classified as occurrence, consistency with the financial statements, completeness, and presentation and disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: occurrence addresses whether transactions/events occurred; consistency addresses derivation from financial statements; completeness addresses inclusion of necessary descriptions and known events/uncertainties; presentation/disclosure addresses classification and disclosure of forward‑looking info. See paragraphs .34‑.38.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation — not expected to test underlying financial statement assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining MD&A, the practitioner is not expected to test the underlying financial statement assertions (e.g., completeness of revenues or existence of inventory) but is responsible for testing completeness of the MD&A explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assurance over underlying statement assertions is obtained through the financial statement audit; MD&A examination focuses on explanations and disclosures. See paragraph .39.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due professional care and professional skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner should exercise due professional care in planning, performing, and evaluating examination procedures and apply an appropriate degree of professional skepticism to obtain reasonable assurance that material misstatements will be detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to all examination procedures; practitioner judgment and skepticism are emphasized. See paragraph .40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures required when performing an examination
rubrics_metrics.description: In an examination of MD&A the practitioner should: obtain understanding of SEC rules and management's method; plan the engagement; consider internal control applicable to MD&A; obtain sufficient evidence including testing completeness; consider subsequent events; obtain written representations; and form an opinion on MD&A as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See paragraphs .41 and cross‑references for detailed procedures (.42‑.66, .110‑.112, .67).

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning considerations — factors to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: When planning, consider industry matters, knowledge of internal control from audits, business matters (organization, capital structure, distribution), information provided externally (press releases, analyst presentations), how performance is analyzed internally, management's SEC knowledge, intended use for nonpublic entities, preliminary judgments about materiality and inherent risk, fraud risk factors, evidential matter types/extent, complex matters requiring specialists, and presence of internal audit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors shape overall strategy, scope, and procedures. See paragraph .42 and following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple components judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the entity has multiple components (locations, branches, subsidiaries), the practitioner should determine which components to test based on relative importance to MD&A disclosure, centralization of records, effectiveness of controls, nature/extent of operations, and similarity across components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider consistency between audit base of components and MD&A disclosures; coordinate audit work with components that will be disclosed. See paragraph .46.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialist's work
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex or subjective matters potentially material to MD&A that require skills other than accounting/auditing, the practitioner may use a specialist and must comply with PCAOB requirements for using specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include engineering determinations of plant production capacity. See paragraph .47.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and understanding of internal control applicable to MD&A preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner should obtain an understanding of internal control related to preparing MD&A sufficient to plan the engagement and assess control risk; relevant controls may include control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information/communication, and monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls over gathering information and nonfinancial data can be relevant. The understanding is used to identify types of potential misstatements and to design tests. See paragraphs .49‑.52.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing completeness of MD&A disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner should obtain sufficient evidence about completeness, for example testing that descriptions of transactions, trends, events, and uncertainties necessary for understanding financial condition, results of operations, liquidity, and capital resources are included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing completeness may include inquiries, analytical procedures, inspection of minutes and records, and corroborative procedures as appropriate to examination scope. See paragraphs .59‑.64.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of subsequent events
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner should consider the effect of events subsequent to the balance-sheet date on MD&A and extend procedures as necessary (for example, when practitioner's report is included in a 1933 Act document, extend procedures up to the effective date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to AS 2905 and AS 4101 for related responsibilities when reports are included in registration statements. See paragraphs .65‑.66 and footnotes .23‑.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining written representations from management
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner should obtain written representations concerning management's responsibility for MD&A, completeness of minutes, events subsequent to the balance-sheet date, and other matters the practitioner deems appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to AS 2805 for timing and signatories of representation letters and AS 4101 for updates when included in filings. See paragraphs .110‑.112 and footnote .31.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming and expressing opinion on MD&A
rubrics_metrics.description: After performing required procedures and obtaining sufficient evidence, the practitioner forms an opinion on whether MD&A includes, in all material respects, the required SEC elements, whether historical amounts were accurately derived, and whether underlying information provides a reasonable basis for disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion considers all material aspects and may be modified if scope limitations or material misstatements exist. Examples and report language are provided in appendices. See paragraph .67 and Appendix A‑C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review engagement procedures and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A review consists principally of applying analytical procedures and making inquiries of persons responsible for financial, accounting, and operational matters; it ordinarily does not include inspection, observation, confirmation, or obtaining corroborating evidential matter; it may bring significant matters to attention but does not provide assurance of detection of all significant matters that an examination would disclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A review provides limited assurance and the report should include appropriate restriction language when not intended for SEC filing. See paragraph .08 and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review acceptance conditions for interim and annual periods
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may accept a review of public entity MD&A for an annual period only if the practitioner has audited the latest annual period and prior periods were audited by the practitioner or predecessor; for interim period reviews, certain additional conditions apply (e.g., review of comparative interim periods under SSARS/AS 4105 or audit of interim FS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonpublic entities choosing to prepare MD&A must have audited annual FS for periods covered and provide written assertion that presentation follows SEC rules; reviewer must consider prior-year audit/review status. See paragraphs .09‑.14.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting restrictions and use limitation for review reports
rubrics_metrics.description: A review report is not intended to be filed with the SEC as a 1933/1934 Act report and should contain a statement restricting use of the report to specified parties if (a) the entity is a public entity or (b) a nonpublic entity making or having made an offering of securities and it appears the securities may be registered or subject to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include restrictions on use and appropriate language; see paragraph .85k (footnote references) and appendices for example report language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predecessor auditor considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a predecessor auditor has audited prior periods covered by MD&A, the successor practitioner should consider whether they can acquire sufficient knowledge of the business and accounting practices for such periods to identify potential material misstatements, perform necessary procedures, and form opinions; review predecessor's working papers as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to paragraphs .07, .10 and .99‑.101 for guidance on acquiring knowledge and reviewing predecessor workpapers and implications for acceptance and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special reporting circumstances (subsequent to filing, other auditors, other information)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard includes guidance for when a practitioner is engaged subsequent to the filing of MD&A, when another auditor audits a significant part of the financial statements, and on responsibility for other information in documents containing MD&A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner should follow specific paragraphs (.92‑.106) addressing these circumstances, including whether to extend procedures or refer to other auditor's reports and how to respond to material inconsistencies with other information.
